questions.stem: The main feature that distinguishes monopolistic competition from perfect competition is

options.text: the number of firms in the industry
the existence of barriers to entry

questions.explanation: Both structures have many firms and free entry, and both leave firms with only normal profit in the long run. The one thing that changes is that products are differentiated by brand, packaging, quality or location, which is what gives each firm slight control over its own price.

distractorRationale.a: Both structures are characterised by a large number of firms
distractorRationale.c: Entry is free in both; barriers belong to oligopoly and monopoly
distractorRationale.d: Free entry means only normal profit survives in the long run under both structures

questions.stem: Heavy advertising is a normal feature of monopolistic competition because

options.text: firms must persuade buyers that their brand differs from close substitutes
there are only a few firms in the industry
buyers have perfect knowledge of all prices
the government requires firms to publicise their prices

questions.explanation: Differentiation only earns a firm loyal customers if buyers believe in it. Advertising builds that belief, which shifts the firm's demand curve outwards and makes it less elastic. Under perfect competition, where goods are identical, advertising would be pure waste.

distractorRationale.b: A few firms describes oligopoly; monopolistic competition has many firms
distractorRationale.c: Perfect knowledge is an assumption of perfect competition, where advertising is pointless
distractorRationale.d: There is no such requirement; advertising here is a commercial strategy, not a legal duty

questions.stem: A market dominated by only two large firms is called
questions.explanation: Duopoly is the special case of oligopoly with exactly two sellers. Interdependence is at its sharpest here, since each firm need only watch one rival to predict the whole market's reaction.

distractorRationale.b: A bilateral monopoly is one seller facing one buyer, which is a different situation
distractorRationale.c: A monopsony is a market with a single buyer, not two sellers
distractorRationale.d: A cartel is a formal agreement among firms to fix price or output, which may or may not involve only two firms

questions.stem: Prices in an oligopolistic market tend to remain unchanged for long periods mainly because

options.text: each firm fears that a price cut will be matched by rivals while a price rise will not be followed
the government fixes the price of the product by law
the firms face perfectly elastic demand curves
production costs in oligopolistic industries never change

questions.explanation: This is the reasoning behind the kinked demand curve. A price cut is matched, so the firm gains few extra customers but earns less on each sale. A price rise is not matched, so the firm loses customers to rivals. Both directions look unattractive, so the price stays put and competition shifts to advertising instead.

distractorRationale.b: Price rigidity in oligopoly arises from the firms' own strategic caution, not from legislation
distractorRationale.c: Perfectly elastic demand belongs to the price taker in perfect competition
distractorRationale.d: Costs certainly do change; rigidity means prices fail to follow those cost changes promptly

questions.stem: An agreement among a few large firms to fix output and price so as to act like a single seller is known as
questions.explanation: A cartel is collusion between independent firms which continue to exist separately but coordinate price or output quotas to raise joint profit. OPEC, of which Nigeria has been a member since 1971, allocates production quotas to its members in exactly this way.

distractorRationale.b: A merger fuses firms into one legal entity, so they no longer need to agree with each other
distractorRationale.c: A subsidy is a government payment to producers and has nothing to do with collusion
distractorRationale.d: A conglomerate is a single firm operating in unrelated industries

questions.stem: In which market structure does the individual firm have absolutely no control over the price of its product?
questions.explanation: Only the perfectly competitive firm is a pure price taker. Its output is a negligible share of total supply and its product is identical to everyone else's, so it must accept the ruling price. In each of the other three structures the firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve and therefore has some price-setting power.

distractorRationale.a: Brand loyalty gives a monopolistically competitive firm slight control over price
distractorRationale.b: An oligopolist has considerable power over price, though it is constrained by rivals' reactions
distractorRationale.d: The monopolist has the greatest control of all, limited only by market demand

questions.stem: In the long run, a firm under monopolistic competition earns only normal profit.
questions.explanation: True. Entry into monopolistic competition is free, so abnormal profit attracts new brands. Each newcomer takes a slice of the existing firms' custom until profit falls to the normal level. Differentiation gives a firm control over price, but it does not protect its profit.

distractorRationale.b: This confuses monopolistic competition with monopoly, where blocked entry allows abnormal profit to persist

questions.stem: Which THREE of the following are forms of non-price competition typically used by oligopolists?

options.text: Extended warranties and free after-sales service
Selling below average variable cost indefinitely
Attractive packaging and frequent product restyling
Publishing a schedule of discounted prices every week

questions.explanation: Non-price competition means attracting customers by any means other than cutting price. Advertising, warranties and after-sales service, and packaging or restyling all fit, because each raises the perceived value of the product while leaving the price alone.

distractorRationale.c: Selling below average variable cost indefinitely would bankrupt the firm and is not a competitive strategy
distractorRationale.e: Publishing weekly discounts is price competition, the very thing oligopolists try to avoid

questions.stem: One characteristic of monopolistic competition is that firms sell products that are
questions.explanation: In monopolistic competition, firms offer differentiated products that are similar but not identical. This differentiation allows firms to have some control over their pricing and marketing strategies.

distractorRationale.a: Identical products are characteristic of perfect competition.
distractorRationale.b: Homogeneous products are not a feature of monopolistic competition.
distractorRationale.d: Perfect substitutes imply no differentiation, which contradicts monopolistic competition.

questions.stem: In oligopoly, firms are said to be interdependent because

options.text: they all produce the same product
the actions of one firm directly affect the others
they operate in a perfectly competitive market

questions.explanation: In an oligopoly, the few firms that dominate the market must consider the potential reactions of their competitors when making pricing and output decisions. This interdependence is a defining characteristic of oligopolistic markets.

distractorRationale.a: Producing the same product is not true for all oligopolists, as they may have differentiated offerings.
distractorRationale.c: Firms in oligopoly typically have significant market power.
distractorRationale.d: Oligopoly is distinct from perfect competition, where firms are price takers.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes price rigidity in oligopoly?

options.text: Prices are flexible and change frequently
Prices remain stable despite changes in demand
Prices are set by the government
Prices are determined by market forces only

questions.explanation: Price rigidity in oligopoly refers to the tendency of prices to remain stable even when market conditions change. This occurs because firms are reluctant to change prices for fear of losing market share to competitors.

distractorRationale.a: Flexible pricing contradicts the concept of price rigidity.
distractorRationale.c: Government intervention is not a defining feature of oligopolistic pricing.
distractorRationale.d: While market forces play a role, inter-firm dynamics significantly influence pricing in oligopoly.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of monopolistic competition?

options.text: Firms have some control over price
There are many firms producing identical products

questions.explanation: In monopolistic competition, firms have some degree of market power, allowing them to influence prices due to product differentiation. This contrasts with perfect competition, where firms are price takers.

distractorRationale.a: Barriers to entry are low in monopolistic competition.
distractorRationale.c: Products are differentiated, not homogeneous.
distractorRationale.d: Firms produce similar but not identical products.

questions.stem: Collusion among firms in an oligopoly is primarily aimed at
questions.explanation: Collusion occurs when firms in an oligopoly cooperate to set prices or output levels to maximize their joint profits, often at the expense of consumer welfare. This behavior can lead to higher prices and reduced competition.

distractorRationale.a: Collusion reduces competition rather than increasing it.
distractorRationale.b: Firms collude to increase prices, not reduce them.
distractorRationale.d: Collusion does not aim to eliminate differentiation but to control pricing strategies.

questions.stem: In which market structure do firms face a downward-sloping demand curve?
questions.explanation: In monopolistic competition, firms face a downward-sloping demand curve due to product differentiation, allowing them to set prices above marginal cost. This is unlike perfect competition, where firms are price takers.

distractorRationale.a: Firms in perfect competition face a horizontal demand curve.
distractorRationale.c: Oligopoly firms may also face a downward-sloping demand curve, but it varies based on competition.
distractorRationale.d: Only monopolistic competition consistently features a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of oligopoly?

options.text: Price competition is the only strategy

questions.explanation: In oligopoly, firms often engage in non-price competition, such as advertising and product differentiation, rather than relying solely on price competition. This helps maintain market share without triggering price wars.

distractorRationale.a: The presence of few large firms is a defining characteristic of oligopoly.
distractorRationale.b: Product differentiation can exist in oligopolistic markets.
distractorRationale.d: Interdependence is a key feature of oligopoly, affecting firm behavior.

questions.stem: In monopolistic competition, firms can earn economic profits in the short run because

options.text: there are no barriers to entry

questions.explanation: Firms in monopolistic competition can earn economic profits in the short run due to their ability to differentiate products, allowing them to charge higher prices than marginal cost. However, in the long run, new entrants erode these profits.

distractorRationale.a: While there are low barriers to entry, it is the product differentiation that allows for short-run profits.
distractorRationale.b: Homogeneous products are characteristic of perfect competition.
distractorRationale.d: Firms in monopolistic competition do not face perfect competition due to product differentiation.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a price war in an oligopoly?

options.text: A situation where firms cooperate to set prices
A situation where firms lower prices to gain market share
A situation where prices remain stable
A situation where firms increase prices simultaneously

questions.explanation: A price war occurs when firms in an oligopoly aggressively lower prices to outcompete each other for market share. This can lead to reduced profits for all firms involved and destabilize the market.

distractorRationale.a: Cooperation among firms is contrary to a price war.
distractorRationale.c: Stable prices are not indicative of a price war.
distractorRationale.d: Simultaneous price increases do not constitute a price war.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common form of non-price competition in monopolistic competition?
questions.explanation: Product advertising is a common form of non-price competition in monopolistic competition. Firms use advertising to highlight the unique features of their products and attract consumers without changing prices.

distractorRationale.a: Lowering prices is a direct price competition strategy, not non-price competition.
distractorRationale.c: Market entry barriers are not a form of competition.
distractorRationale.d: Collusion is more characteristic of oligopoly than monopolistic competition.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors can lead to price rigidity in an oligopoly?
questions.explanation: Price rigidity in oligopoly often arises from firms' fear of losing market share. If one firm lowers prices, others may follow, leading to a price war, so firms prefer to keep prices stable.

distractorRationale.a: High competition typically leads to price adjustments, not rigidity.
distractorRationale.c: Low barriers to entry would not necessarily cause price rigidity.
distractorRationale.d: Excess supply usually leads to price reductions, not stability.

questions.stem: A characteristic of monopolistic competition is that firms have some control over their prices due to

options.text: the identical nature of their products
the presence of a few dominant firms

questions.explanation: In monopolistic competition, firms differentiate their products, which allows them to have some control over their pricing. This differentiation can be based on quality, features, or branding, leading to a downward-sloping demand curve for each firm's product.

distractorRationale.a: Identical products would lead to perfect competition, not monopolistic competition.
distractorRationale.c: Advertising is often a key strategy in monopolistic competition to highlight product differences.
distractorRationale.d: Having a few dominant firms is more characteristic of oligopoly rather than monopolistic competition.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of oligopoly?
questions.explanation: Oligopoly is characterized by a few firms that are interdependent, meaning the actions of one firm can significantly affect the others. This interdependence can lead to collusion or strategic behavior among firms.

distractorRationale.a: Many small firms are characteristic of perfect competition.
distractorRationale.b: Product homogeneity is more typical in perfect competition or pure oligopoly, but oligopoly may also involve differentiated products.
distractorRationale.d: Perfect information is a feature of perfect competition, not oligopoly.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the concept of price rigidity in oligopoly?

options.text: Firms frequently change prices to attract customers
Firms are reluctant to change prices due to fear of price wars
Prices are always set at marginal cost
Firms have no control over their prices

questions.explanation: Price rigidity occurs in oligopoly because firms are hesitant to change prices, fearing that competitors will respond with price cuts, leading to a price war. This results in stable prices despite changes in demand or costs.

distractorRationale.a: Frequent price changes are not typical in oligopoly due to the risk of retaliation from competitors.
distractorRationale.c: Prices in oligopoly are not always set at marginal cost due to the presence of market power.
distractorRationale.d: Firms in oligopoly do have some control over prices, unlike in perfect competition.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes collusion in an oligopoly?

options.text: A legal agreement to set prices
An illegal agreement to fix prices
A strategy to increase market share
A method to enhance product differentiation

questions.explanation: Collusion in an oligopoly refers to an illegal agreement among firms to fix prices or limit production to maximize profits. This practice is often scrutinized by regulatory bodies due to its anti-competitive nature.

distractorRationale.a: Collusion is typically illegal and not a formal legal agreement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason for price rigidity in oligopoly?
questions.explanation: High elasticity of demand would typically encourage firms to change prices in response to market conditions. In contrast, fear of price wars, collusion, and interdependence among firms are reasons for price rigidity in oligopoly.

distractorRationale.a: Fear of price wars is a significant reason for price rigidity.
distractorRationale.b: Collusive agreements directly contribute to maintaining stable prices.
distractorRationale.d: Interdependence among firms leads to cautious pricing strategies to avoid triggering competitive responses.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the demand curve faced by a firm in monopolistic competition?
questions.explanation: A firm in monopolistic competition faces a downward-sloping demand curve due to product differentiation, which allows it to have some control over its price. This means that as the firm lowers its price, it can increase the quantity demanded.

distractorRationale.a: Perfectly elastic demand is characteristic of perfect competition, not monopolistic competition.
distractorRationale.b: Perfectly inelastic demand would imply no change in quantity demanded regardless of price, which is not the case here.
distractorRationale.d: A vertical demand curve indicates no response to price changes, which does not apply in monopolistic competition.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a potential outcome of collusion in an oligopoly?
questions.explanation: Collusion among firms in an oligopoly often leads to higher prices for consumers, as firms agree to set prices above the competitive level to maximize their joint profits. This reduces consumer welfare and can lead to market inefficiencies.

distractorRationale.a: Collusion reduces competition, as firms work together rather than competing.
distractorRationale.c: Collusion typically increases market power among the participating firms.
distractorRationale.d: Firms involved in collusion often see higher profits due to reduced competition.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the concept of interdependence in oligopoly?

options.text: Firms do not consider the actions of other firms.
Firms' pricing and output decisions depend on competitors' actions.

questions.explanation: In an oligopoly, the decisions made by one firm affect the decisions of others, leading to interdependence. This means that firms must consider the potential reactions of their competitors when setting prices or output levels.

distractorRationale.a: This statement is incorrect as interdependence means firms do consider each other.
distractorRationale.b: Independent pricing decisions are characteristic of perfect competition, not oligopoly.
